To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the source of N in a supplement fed to sheep consuming a high-concent-rate diet had no large effect on feed intake or on postabsorptive nitrogen flux across the liver or the splanchnic region of the sheep.

feeding supplemental urea, soybean meal, or blood feather meal to sheep fed a high-grain diet ad libituum did not affect nutrient intake, nutrient digestaibility, or nitrogen metabolism in sheep fed ad libitum.
sheep fed high-concentrate rations ad libitum consumed 1.2 kg of feed per day, digested 90% of the feed DM, and absorbed 90% of feed N as alpha-amino N.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of dietary nitrogen on nutrient utilization in sheep consuming high-concentration diets ad libitium.
the effect of supplemental dietary N on feed intake, N metabolism, and energy balance in ruminants.
the effect of dietary nitrogen on feed intake, nitrogen flux across the splanchnic tissue and nitrogen metabolism in sheep consuming a high concentrate diet ad lib.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the addition of supplemental N in the form of either urea or protein to a high-concentrated diet for ad lib feeding had no large influence on nutrient digestibility or postabsorptive metabolism in sheep.
the source of N did not influence feed intake, digesta flow, nutrient digestibility or blood flow.
N supplementation did not influence feed intake or nutrient digestibility, or the postabsorptive flux of alpha-amino acids, ammonia N, and urea N across the PDV, hepate, or splan-chnic tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sheep consuming high-concentration diets ad libitium can tolerate a wide range of supplemental N without adverse effects on intake and digestion or N metabolism.
the source of N supplementation had no large effects, and that supplemental N had large effects.
the addition of supplemental N to a high-concentrated diet for ad lib consumption by sheep did not increase feed intake and had little effect on N utilization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the source of dietary nitrogen (protein or non-protein) did not influence the post-absorptive metabolism of nitrogen in sheep consuming high-concentration diets ad libitium.
sheep fed a 95% high concentrate diet ad lib can tolerate a 50% increase in dietary CP (6.6 vs. 11.4%) without any detrimental effects on feed intake, DM digestibility, N balance, or N utilization.
